_readme: Frozen snapshot of the static content that data/*.ts and content/blog/*.mdx held
immediately before the database migration. scripts/import-content.mjs reads this
file; it does not read the TypeScript modules, because a .mjs script cannot
resolve their @/ path aliases and a snapshot is reviewable in a way that a
runtime import is not.
Editorial decisions baked into this snapshot, all of them driven by the rule
that placeholder text must never be published:
* Project case-study bodies were the string 'Detailed case-study documentation
is being prepared.' repeated across nine fields. They are imported as EMPTY
content. The case-study component already renders that exact sentence as its
empty state, so the public page is unchanged while the database holds no
fake prose. Project metadata (title, category, summary, technologies, image)
is real and is published, preserving the live site.
* The one blog post is imported as a DRAFT. Its body says 'Draft note - this
article is a placeholder for final editorial content', and it carried
draft: true in data/blog.ts. Its leading '# Building Useful Systems' heading
is dropped: the page renders the title in its own <h1>, and keeping it was
the duplicate-H1 defect.
* Experience periods were the literal string 'Details pending confirmation'.
No dates are invented. start_date is null and the timeline simply renders no
period line. Everything else about these entries is real, so they are
published.
* Certification issue dates were the same placeholder. issue_date is null,
which renders as an em dash. Titles and issuers are real, so they are
published.
* Engagement tiers reproduce data/pricing.ts exactly, including the rendered
price strings 'Starting from $150', 'Custom Quote' and "Let's Discuss".

posts.title: Building Useful Systems
posts.excerpt: A draft note on turning complex requirements into software people can rely on.
posts.content:
> Draft note — this article is a placeholder for final editorial content.

Software should make a real workflow clearer, safer, or more capable. The implementation details matter, but they are in service of the people who depend on the system.

The strongest implementations usually begin with a small, observable improvement: a clearer decision, a safer handoff, or a workflow that no longer depends on tribal knowledge.
